title: Questioning the ability of feature-based explanations to empower non-experts in robo-advised financial decision-making
authors: Bertrand, A.; Maxwell, W.; Eagan, J. R.
venue: 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '23)
tldr: A qualitative and large-scale quantitative study found that feature-based explanations from a robo-advisor do not improve non-expert users' understanding or appropriate reliance, and dialogic formats can increase harmful over-trust.
problem_and_motivation: European financial legislation requires robo-advisors to explain recommendations so clients make informed decisions, yet few studies have examined whether mandated feature-based explanations actually help non-expert users.
approach: Built Robex, a simplified life-insurance robo-advisor using Ecological Interface Design with a rule-based recommendation algorithm and SHAP-based feature importance explanations.
Conducted qualitative interviews with 11 participants: 6 French financial consumer protection regulators and 5 novice end-users.
Designed three hybrid explanation formats—graphical-static, graphical-mutable, and dialogic—varying the balance between textual and visual representation of feature importances.
Ran a large-scale between-subjects experiment with 256 French participants recruited via Lucid, crossing four explanation conditions with correct and incorrect recommendations.
Measured reliance, trust (McKnight framework), cognitive load (NASA-TLX), user engagement, and objective understanding via test questions and ANOVA analysis.
findings: num: The no-explanation control group was more or equally likely to distinguish good from bad advice compared to all explanation groups.
num: Dialogic explanations increased trust in incorrect recommendations significantly (p=0.001) compared to no explanation, leading to harmful over-reliance.
num: Graphical-mutable explanations showed a non-significant tendency (p=0.1) toward better understanding of the recommendation than other conditions.
num: No statistically significant effect of explanation format on cognitive load or user engagement, with average perceived cognitive workload at 5.6 out of 10.
Regulators and end-users expressed divergent explanation needs: regulators prioritized risk communication and completeness, while users wanted simplicity and engagement.
key_figures_tables: Figure 2: Three explanation interfaces (graphical-static, graphical-mutable, dialogic) -> Graphical uses arrow-based feature importances; dialogic mimics SMS chat.
Figure 3: Experimental workflow showing profiling, recommendation, explanation, and decision phases -> Replicates real robo-advisor interaction flow.
Table 1: Themes from regulator and end-user interviews on explanation format and purpose -> Regulators emphasize risk warning; users want simplicity.
Table 2: Questionnaire items with Cronbach's alphas for trust (0.854, 0.878), engagement (0.818), and cognitive load (0.829) -> Validated measurement instruments.

definitions.definition: Simplified, fictional life-insurance robo-advisor built for the study using Ecological Interface Design.
SHapley Additive exPlanations; a post-hoc, model-agnostic interpretability method providing feature importance values.
Explanations that link user characteristics to the AI recommendation by showing how each input feature contributed to the output.
Conversational, SMS-like textual explanation format presenting feature importances as chat messages.
Following an incorrect AI recommendation without adequate critical evaluation.
General Data Protection Regulation; EU law requiring disclosure of meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decisions.

topics.name: Landscape of Existing Personal Finance Systems
topics.justification: Discusses the current state of robo-advisors in France and Europe, noting most are rule-based with poor explanations.

topics.name: Limitations and Gaps in Existing Systems
topics.justification: Identifies that existing robo-advisor explanations are generic and fail to link recommendations to user characteristics.

topics.name: User Trust in Personal Finance Systems
topics.justification: Directly measures and analyzes user trust in robo-advisor recommendations across explanation formats.

topics.name: Engagement Dynamics in Personal Finance Applications
topics.justification: Measures user engagement with explanation interfaces but finds no significant effect across conditions.

topics.name: Evaluation of Algorithmic Modules
topics.justification: Evaluates SHAP-based feature importance explanations for their effectiveness in supporting non-expert financial decision-making.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides empirical evidence that legally mandated feature-based explanations do not improve non-expert users' understanding or appropriate reliance on financial AI recommendations compared to no explanation at all.
directly_justifies: Feature-based explanations do not improve appropriate reliance or understanding compared to no explanation.
Dialogic explanations significantly increase trust in incorrect recommendations (p=0.001), causing harmful over-reliance.
Regulators and end-users have divergent perspectives on explanation needs, with regulators emphasizing risk and users wanting simplicity.
No significant effect of explanation format on cognitive load or user engagement.
limits: Study used a simplified, fictional robo-advisor rather than a real AI system or real financial products.
Non-expert qualitative study participants were graduate students, a narrow demographic subset.
Content analysis was based on one author's interview notes rather than full transcripts.
Average participant financial knowledge was low (1.3/5), limiting generalizability to more financially literate users.

limitations: Study used a simplified, fictional robo-advisor rather than a real AI-powered system or real financial products.
Qualitative study participants were graduate students, a narrow demographic representing non-experts.
Content analysis performed on one author's interview notes rather than full transcripts, limiting data richness.
Participants could not interact with real financial advisors for comparison.
Average participant financial knowledge was low (1.3 out of 5), limiting generalizability to more financially literate populations.
Study conducted exclusively in France, limiting cross-cultural generalizability.
remember_this: Feature-based explanations do not improve non-expert users' understanding or appropriate reliance compared to no explanation.
Dialogic explanations significantly increase trust in incorrect recommendations, leading to harmful over-reliance (p=0.001).
Graphical explanation formats may be better suited than dialogic formats for informing clients about risk.
Regulators and end-users have divergent explanation needs, with regulators emphasizing risk and users wanting simplicity.
Average participant financial knowledge was 1.3 out of 5, confirming non-expert status.
